Predict the surface roughness. For turning with a round-nose tool: Ra (theoretical) = f^2 / (32 * r_nose) where r_nose is the tool nose radius. The actual Ra is typically 1.5-3x the theoretical due to built-up edge, vibration, and material smearing. For milling: Ra depends on feed per tooth, cutter geometry, and axial depth. For grinding: Ra is determined by wheel grit size, dress parameters, and table speed.

Check for chatter stability. The critical depth of cut for chatter depends on the dynamic stiffness of the machine-tool-workpiece system and the specific cutting force of the material. Use the stability lobe diagram if available (measured from tap tests on the actual setup). If chatter occurs at the desired parameters, adjust: reduce depth of cut, change speed to a stable lobe, increase tool overhang stiffness, or add damping.

steps.description: Select the cutting tool geometry, coating, and grade for the operation, and establish the tool life monitoring and replacement strategy.

inputs.name: cutting-parameters
inputs.desc: Optimized speed, feed, and depth of cut

inputs.name: workpiece-specification
inputs.desc: Material being machined and operation type

outputs.name: tool-specification
outputs.desc: Insert geometry (CNMG, WNMG, etc.), grade (substrate + coating), chipbreaker selection, and tool holder specification

outputs.name: tool-management-plan
outputs.desc: Tool life criterion (flank wear limit, surface finish degradation, dimensional drift), replacement strategy (fixed interval or condition-based), and preset/offset procedure

process: Select the insert grade (substrate + coating) for the work material. For steel turning: CVD-coated carbide (TiCN + Al2O3 + TiN multilayer) for general purpose. PVD-coated for finishing (sharper edge, thinner coating). Cermet for high-speed finishing of steel (excellent surface finish). For stainless steel: PVD-coated carbide with a sharp geometry to reduce work hardening. For nickel alloys (Inconel): uncoated or PVD-coated carbide with high cobalt content for thermal resistance, or ceramic inserts (SiAlON, whisker-reinforced alumina) at much higher speeds.

Select the insert geometry. Negative rake inserts (CNMG, WNMG, SNMG) for roughing (strongest edge, double-sided = more cutting edges). Positive rake inserts (CCMT, DCMT) for finishing (lower cutting forces, better surface finish). The nose radius affects both strength and surface finish: larger radius = stronger edge and smoother finish but higher radial force. Chipbreaker selection: open for roughing (heavy feed), medium for general purpose, close for finishing (light feed).

Set the tool life criterion. For roughing: flank wear VB_max = 0.3mm or notch wear VN = 0.6mm. For finishing: the tool is replaced when the surface finish exceeds the specification or the dimensional drift exceeds the tolerance band. Measure the dimensional drift trend by SPC to establish the predictable tool wear pattern and set the replacement interval conservatively within the drift envelope.

Establish the tool presetting procedure. Measure tool length and diameter offsets on a tool presetter (off-machine measurement) to minimize setup time. For precision work, perform a test cut and adjust the offset based on the measured dimension. For CNC machines, use tool wear compensation to automatically adjust the offset as the tool wears (step adjustment per part or continuous compensation from in-process measurement).

steps.description: Verify that the machining process is capable of consistently producing parts within specification through statistical analysis and measurement system evaluation.

inputs.name: cutting-parameters
inputs.desc: Finalized machining parameters

inputs.name: workpiece-specification
inputs.desc: Dimensional tolerances and surface finish requirements to verify capability against

outputs.name: capability-assessment
outputs.desc: Process capability indices (Cp, Cpk) for each critical dimension, with histogram and control chart data

outputs.name: measurement-system-analysis
outputs.desc: Gage R&R results for the measurement system used to assess capability (acceptable if %GRR < 10% of tolerance for critical dimensions, < 30% for non-critical)

process: First validate the measurement system. Perform a gage R&R study (AIAG MSA method) with 10 parts, 3 operators, 3 repeats. Calculate %GRR as a percentage of the tolerance. If %GRR > 30%, the measurement system is inadequate; improve the gage before assessing process capability. For CMM measurements, verify the probe qualification, fixturing repeatability, and thermal compensation.

Run a capability study. Machine a minimum of 30 consecutive parts under normal production conditions (include tool changes, reloads, thermal variations). Measure each critical dimension. Calculate Cp = (USL - LSL) / (6 * sigma) and Cpk = min((USL - mean) / (3 * sigma), (mean - LSL) / (3 * sigma)). For most manufacturing: Cpk > 1.33 is acceptable, Cpk > 1.67 for safety-critical dimensions, Cpk > 2.0 for zero-defect targets.

If Cpk is below target, diagnose the cause. Low Cp (process variation too wide): investigate sources of variation (thermal drift, tool wear, fixture clamping variation, material hardness variation, spindle bearing play). Low Cpk with adequate Cp (process not centered): adjust the tool offset to center the process. Use X-bar and R control charts to distinguish between common cause and special cause variation.

Implement ongoing process control. Set SPC control limits from the capability study data. Monitor key dimensions on a control chart basis (every nth part, or 100% for critical characteristics). Define the control plan: measurement method, frequency, sample size, reaction plan for out-of-control conditions. For high-precision work (tolerances below 10 microns), environmental control (temperature within 1C of 20C) and warm-up protocols (run the machine for 30+ minutes before production) are required.

description: Design a semiconductor fabrication process module from lithography through etch and deposition to defect management and yield optimization.

steps.description: Design the lithography process step for pattern definition including resist selection, exposure conditions, and resolution enhancement techniques.

inputs.name: design-rules
inputs.desc: Minimum feature size (critical dimension), pitch, and overlay requirements for the layer being patterned

inputs.name: available-equipment
inputs.desc: Lithography platform (ArF immersion 193nm, EUV 13.5nm, i-line 365nm) and its optical parameters (NA, partial coherence)

outputs.name: lithography-recipe
outputs.desc: Complete lithography recipe: resist type and thickness, soft bake, exposure dose and focus, PEB, develop time, and any resolution enhancement techniques

outputs.name: process-window
outputs.desc: Exposure-defocus (ED) window showing the common depth of focus across the critical features, with the process margin for dose and focus variation

process: Calculate the resolution limit: R = k1 * lambda / NA, where lambda is the wavelength, NA is the numerical aperture, and k1 is the process factor (theoretical minimum 0.25 for single exposure, practical minimum 0.3-0.4). For 193nm immersion with NA = 1.35: minimum half-pitch approximately 38nm at k1 = 0.27 (requires multiple patterning). For EUV at 13.5nm with NA = 0.33: minimum half-pitch approximately 13nm at k1 = 0.32.

Select the resist. For advanced nodes: chemically amplified resist (CAR) for ArF, metal oxide or CAR for EUV. Resist thickness follows the aspect ratio limit (height / width < 3:1 to avoid pattern collapse). For fine features, thinner resist (50-100nm for sub-50nm features) with hard mask underneath. Characterize the resist contrast curve (remaining thickness vs log dose) to determine the optimal exposure dose (dose to clear for positive resist, dose to print for the target CD).

Apply optical proximity correction (OPC) to the mask. Sub-resolution assist features (SRAFs) improve the depth of focus for isolated features. Serif and hammerhead corrections for line-end pullback and corner rounding. Inverse lithography technology (ILT) for the most critical layers. Verify the OPC by aerial image simulation and check the mask error enhancement factor (MEEF): MEEF = (delta_CD_wafer / delta_CD_mask) * (1/M) where M is the reduction ratio (typically 4x).

Measure the process window. Expose a focus-exposure matrix (FEM) on a test wafer. Measure the CD at each dose-focus combination. Plot the Bossung curves (CD vs focus at constant dose). The usable process window is the overlap of all features being within their CD specification across the dose and focus range. Minimum acceptable depth of focus is typically 100-200nm for ArF immersion (must accommodate wafer topography, focus error, and tilt).

steps.description: Design the plasma etch process for pattern transfer from the resist into the target film, achieving the required profile, selectivity, and uniformity.

inputs.name: lithography-recipe
inputs.desc: Resist pattern with CD and profile to be transferred

inputs.name: film-stack
inputs.desc: Target film and underlying layers to etch through (material, thickness) with selectivity requirements

outputs.name: etch-recipe
outputs.desc: Etch chemistry (gas mixtures, pressures, power levels), endpoint detection method, and over-etch strategy

outputs.name: etch-performance
outputs.desc: Achieved etch rate, selectivity to mask and underlayer, CD bias, profile angle, uniformity, and loading effects

process: Select the etch chemistry from the material. Silicon and polysilicon: Cl2/HBr-based (Cl2 for high rate, HBr for selectivity to oxide and profile control, add O2 for sidewall passivation). Silicon dioxide: C4F8/Ar/O2 (fluorocarbon polymer deposition on the sidewall provides anisotropy, O2 removes excess polymer, Ar provides ion bombardment for vertical etch). Silicon nitride: CH2F2/O2 or CHF3/O2 (selective to oxide by tuning the C:F ratio). Metals (TiN, W): Cl2/BCl3 for TiN, SF6/Cl2 for W.

Balance anisotropy and selectivity. Anisotropic etching requires a passivation mechanism on the sidewall (polymer deposition from fluorocarbon gases, or oxidation from O2 addition to chlorine chemistry). Higher ion energy (higher bias power) improves anisotropy but reduces selectivity (the mask etches faster). Lower pressure increases ion directionality (more anisotropic) but may increase ion damage to the underlayer.

Implement endpoint detection. Optical emission spectroscopy (OES): monitor the emission line of a volatile etch product (e.g., CO for oxide etch in fluorocarbon, SiCl for silicon etch in chlorine). When the target film is consumed, the etch product signal drops (endpoint). Set the over-etch time as a percentage of the main etch time (typically 20-50%) to clear residual material from topographic features and compensate for across-wafer uniformity variation.

Characterize the etch performance. Measure CD bias (CD_after_etch minus CD_after_litho, including any trim steps). Profile angle by SEM cross-section (target 88-90 degrees for vertical profile). Selectivity = etch rate of target / etch rate of mask (must be sufficient for the mask to survive the entire etch plus over-etch). Uniformity: measure the etch rate at 49 or more points across the wafer (target 3-sigma uniformity below 3%).

steps.description: Design the thin film deposition process for the required film (dielectric, metal, or barrier) with target thickness, composition, and conformality.

inputs.name: film-requirements
inputs.desc: Target film material, thickness, electrical properties (resistivity, dielectric constant, breakdown voltage), and step coverage requirements

inputs.name: thermal-budget
inputs.desc: Maximum process temperature allowed by the device structure (especially for back-end-of-line processes with low-k dielectrics or metal interconnects)

outputs.name: deposition-recipe
outputs.desc: Deposition method (PVD, CVD, ALD, electroplating) with process parameters (temperature, pressure, gas flows, power, pulse timing)

outputs.name: film-characterization
outputs.desc: Measured film properties: thickness and uniformity (by ellipsometry or XRR), composition (by XPS or RBS), resistivity (by four-point probe), stress (by wafer bow), and step coverage (by SEM cross-section)

process: Select the deposition method from the conformality requirement. PVD (sputtering) for blanket metal films where step coverage is not critical (liner/barrier on planar surfaces, seed layers). CVD for conformal films in high-aspect-ratio features (TEOS oxide, tungsten via fill, TiN barrier). ALD for the highest conformality at sub-nm thickness control (required for films below 5nm: high-k gate dielectrics, ALD barrier layers, sub-3nm conformal coatings in extreme aspect ratios above 20:1). Electroplating for copper interconnect fill after PVD seed.

For PVD (sputtering): select the target material and sputtering gas (Ar for most metals). DC sputtering for metals, RF sputtering for insulators. Reactive sputtering (adding N2 or O2 to the Ar) for nitrides and oxides (e.g., TiN from a Ti target in Ar/N2). Ionized PVD (iPVD) for improved step coverage in high-aspect-ratio features (ions are directional, unlike neutral sputtered atoms). Typical deposition rates: 10-100 nm/min depending on power and target-substrate distance.

For CVD: select the precursor chemistry. TEOS (tetraethyl orthosilicate) + O3 for conformal oxide at moderate temperature (400-500C). PECVD SiO2 (SiH4 + N2O, 300-400C) for passivation and interlayer dielectric. PECVD SiN (SiH4 + NH3, 300-400C) for etch stop and barrier. Tungsten CVD (WF6 + H2, 300-450C) for via fill. The film properties (stress, composition, density) are sensitive to the plasma power, pressure, temperature, and gas ratio.

For ALD: define the pulse sequence. Example for Al2O3: TMA (trimethylaluminum) pulse, purge, H2O pulse, purge = 1 ALD cycle depositing approximately 0.1nm per cycle. The process temperature window (between precursor condensation at low T and precursor decomposition at high T) defines the ALD operating regime. For thermal ALD of HfO2 gate dielectric: HfCl4 + H2O at 300C. Plasma-enhanced ALD (PEALD) allows lower temperature and different film properties. Verify the saturation behavior (growth per cycle vs pulse time) to confirm true ALD mode.

Characterize the deposited film. Thickness and uniformity by spectroscopic ellipsometry (49-point map, target uniformity below 2% 3-sigma). Film composition by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) for stoichiometry and impurity levels. Resistivity by four-point probe (for metals and conductive films). Film stress by wafer bow measurement (Stoney equation: stress = Es * ts^2 * (1/R - 1/R0) / (6 * (1 - vs) * tf) where Es, ts, vs are substrate properties and tf is film thickness). High compressive or tensile stress can cause delamination or wafer warp.

steps.description: Manage defect density through inspection, classification, and root cause analysis to achieve and maintain the target yield.

inputs.name: etch-performance
inputs.desc: Etch process characterization data

inputs.name: film-characterization
inputs.desc: Deposition process characterization data

outputs.name: defect-density-map
outputs.desc: Defect density (defects/cm^2) by defect type and process step, with Pareto of top yield-limiting defect types

outputs.name: yield-model
outputs.desc: Yield prediction from defect density using the Poisson model (Y = exp(-D0 * A)) or negative binomial model (Y = (1 + D0 * A / alpha)^(-alpha)) with the process baseline and improvement targets

process: Implement inline defect inspection after each critical process step. Bright-field optical inspection (KLA 2900 series or equivalent) for patterned wafer inspection: detects particles, pattern defects, and bridging down to approximately 30nm depending on the design rule. Dark-field inspection (KLA Surfscan or equivalent) for unpatterned wafer monitoring: measures particle density and haze on bare or film-coated wafers.

Classify defects. Use automated defect classification (ADC) with SEM review of a sample from each defect bin. Common categories: particles (from process tool contamination, wafer handling), pattern defects (bridging from litho, open from etch, CD variations), film defects (pinholes, delamination, nodules), and scratch/handling damage. The Pareto of defect types by count guides the improvement priority.

Calculate the yield impact. For random defects: Y = exp(-D0 * A) where D0 is the defect density (defects/cm^2) at the critical defect size, and A is the die area. A defect must be at a critical location (on a feature, not in a field area) and large enough to cause a functional failure. The critical area analysis (from the layout) determines what fraction of the die area is sensitive to each defect type.

Root-cause and fix. Trace each high-count defect type to its process step by comparing defect maps before and after each step (defect adders per step). Particles: clean the tool (chamber clean, gas line purge), qualify hardware (o-rings, showerheads), improve wafer handling. Pattern defects: adjust litho or etch process (focus/dose, etch chemistry). Systematic defects (repeating at the same die location on every wafer): mask defect or reticle contamination, fix the mask. Track the defect density trend over time to verify that fixes are sustaining.

description: Engineer a surface modification or coating system from requirement definition through process selection and characterization to specification and quality control.

steps.description: Define the surface performance requirements from the application and identify the failure modes the surface treatment must prevent.

inputs.name: application-requirements
inputs.desc: Operating conditions (contact stress, sliding speed, temperature, corrosive media), required life, and substrate material

inputs.name: failure-mode-history
inputs.desc: Current failure modes of uncoated or currently coated parts (wear mechanism, corrosion type, thermal damage)

outputs.name: surface-specification-targets
outputs.desc: Required surface properties: hardness range, friction coefficient, wear rate, corrosion resistance, thermal stability, thickness, and adhesion

outputs.name: candidate-processes
outputs.desc: Short list of surface modification processes capable of meeting the property targets on the substrate material

process: Identify the dominant wear mechanism. Abrasive wear (hard particles sliding against the surface): need high hardness. Adhesive wear (material transfer between sliding surfaces): need low friction and chemical incompatibility. Erosive wear (particle impact): need hardness plus toughness. Fretting wear (micro-motion at contact interfaces): need a combination of hardness and solid lubricant. The wear mechanism dictates the coating property priorities.

Identify corrosion requirements. Oxidation resistance at temperature (need a stable oxide former: alumina from Al, chromia from Cr). Aqueous corrosion resistance (need a barrier coating or cathodic protection). Hot corrosion (sulfate/vanadate attack at 700-900C): need MCrAlY or diffusion aluminide coatings. Hydrogen permeation resistance: need a dense barrier (TiN, TiAlN, or DLC).

Identify process compatibility with the substrate. PVD and CVD work on most substrates but require vacuum. PVD at 200-500C is compatible with tempered steel (no softening if below tempering temperature). CVD at 800-1000C is limited to substrates that tolerate the temperature (HSS, cemented carbide, ceramics). Thermal spray at atmospheric pressure deposits thick coatings (50-500 microns) but with porosity and lower adhesion. Electroplating is substrate-chemistry dependent. Nitriding modifies the substrate surface directly (no separate coating layer).

Short-list 2-3 candidate processes that meet both the property and the process compatibility requirements. For cutting tools: PVD TiAlN or AlCrN for general-purpose, CVD Al2O3 + TiCN for indexable inserts, DLC for non-ferrous machining. For wear-resistant machine components: hard chromium electroplating (being replaced due to Cr(VI) regulations), thermal spray (HVOF WC-Co), or PVD CrN. For corrosion-resistant fasteners: zinc-nickel electroplating, or PVD CrN.

steps.description: Design the coating deposition process including surface preparation, deposition parameters, and post-treatment to achieve the target properties.

inputs.name: candidate-processes
inputs.desc: Short-listed processes from the requirements analysis

inputs.name: surface-specification-targets
inputs.desc: Target properties for the coating

outputs.name: coating-process-specification
outputs.desc: Complete process specification: surface preparation, deposition parameters (temperature, pressure, power, gas composition, rotation), post-treatment, and expected properties

outputs.name: trial-coating-results
outputs.desc: Properties of the trial coating measured on test coupons (hardness, adhesion, thickness, composition, residual stress)

process: Surface preparation. Clean the substrate to remove all contaminants (ultrasonic cleaning in alkaline solution, rinse in DI water, dry). For PVD: sputter etch in the vacuum chamber (Ar ion bombardment at 500-1000V bias for 5-30 minutes) to remove the native oxide and activate the surface. For thermal spray: grit blast to Sa 3 (white metal) with angular alumina (grit size per the coating specification, typically 24-60 mesh) to create anchor tooth profile (Ra 5-15 microns). For electroplating: acid activation per the plating specification.

For PVD (cathodic arc or magnetron sputtering): select the target material (Ti, Cr, Al, or alloy for reactive deposition of TiN, CrN, TiAlN, AlCrN). Set the reactive gas flow (N2 for nitrides, C2H2 for carbides/DLC). Substrate temperature (200-500C), bias voltage (-50 to -200V), and chamber pressure (0.5-5 Pa) control the coating microstructure, hardness, and residual stress. Higher bias gives denser, harder coatings but higher compressive stress (risk of delamination above 4-6 GPa for most substrates).

For HVOF thermal spray (WC-Co, Cr3C2-NiCr): select the spray gun and fuel (kerosene or hydrogen). Particle velocity (600-900 m/s for HVOF) determines the coating density and adhesion. Spray distance (200-400mm), powder feed rate, and traverse speed determine the coating thickness per pass (typically 20-50 microns per pass). Keep the substrate temperature below the tempering temperature of steel substrates (monitor with IR pyrometer during spraying).

Post-treatment. For PVD coatings on cutting tools: typically none required (the coating is used as-deposited). For thermal spray: sealing with a polymer or glass sealant to close surface-connected porosity (required for corrosion applications). For electroplated chromium: baking at 190C for 4+ hours to desorb hydrogen and prevent hydrogen embrittlement of high-strength steel substrates (mandatory per ASTM B850 / AMS 2759/9 for steels above 1000 MPa tensile strength).

Trial coating on test coupons (same material and surface condition as the production parts). Measure: hardness by nanoindentation (ISO 14577, indent depth less than 10% of coating thickness to avoid substrate influence), adhesion by scratch test (ISO 20502, report Lc2 critical load), thickness by calotest (ball cratering) or cross-section SEM, composition by EDS or GD-OES, and residual stress by the substrate curvature method (Stoney equation) or XRD sin-squared-psi method.

steps.description: Validate the coating performance through tribological testing, corrosion testing, and field trial correlation to confirm that it meets the application requirements.

inputs.name: trial-coating-results
inputs.desc: Measured properties of the trial coating

inputs.name: application-requirements
inputs.desc: Operating conditions and target life

outputs.name: performance-test-results
outputs.desc: Tribological test results (friction coefficient, wear rate, wear mechanism), corrosion test results, and any accelerated life test data

outputs.name: coating-specification-document
outputs.desc: Final coating specification for procurement or in-house production, including all acceptance criteria and inspection methods

process: Tribological testing. Pin-on-disc (ASTM G99) for sliding wear: measure the friction coefficient and specific wear rate (mm^3 / N*m) against the specified counter-body material at the relevant speed, load, and temperature. Block-on-ring (ASTM G77) for conforming contact. Reciprocating ball-on-flat (ASTM G133) for fretting or oscillating applications. The test conditions must approximate the application conditions; wear mechanisms change with contact pressure and temperature, so a test at the wrong conditions gives misleading data.

Corrosion testing. Neutral salt spray (ASTM B117) for general atmospheric corrosion resistance (number of hours to red rust or white rust). Electrochemical testing (potentiodynamic polarization per ASTM G5) for quantitative comparison of coatings (corrosion potential, corrosion current density, pitting potential). Immersion testing in the actual service fluid at temperature for process equipment coatings. The test duration and conditions must be relevant to the application; a 500-hour salt spray test on an automotive fastener is meaningful, but on a downhole tool it is not.

Accelerated life testing where feasible. For cutting tools: run the coated tool in the actual machining operation and measure tool life vs the uncoated or current-coating baseline. For wear components: run a bench test that simulates the actual duty cycle at accelerated frequency or load. Correlate the accelerated test results to field life using the known acceleration factor or by comparison to field data from the current coating.

Write the coating specification. Include: coating material and composition, thickness range, hardness range, adhesion minimum (Lc2 or Rockwell indentation per VDI 3198: HF1-HF4 acceptable, HF5-HF6 unacceptable), surface roughness after coating, visual appearance acceptance criteria, and any post-treatment requirements. Reference the applicable standards (ISO 6158 for electroplated chromium, ISO 26443 for PVD coatings, ISO 14919 for thermal spray). Define the lot acceptance test plan: which tests on every lot (thickness, hardness, adhesion on a test coupon) and which tests periodically (full characterization including composition, tribological testing).
